5. Multi-environment trials and genomics

Source: vignettes/flexyBayes-05-met-and-genomics.Rmd
flexyBayes-05-met-and-genomics.Rmd
This page in one panel
The problem
Varieties do not rank the same everywhere. Separating a variety’s general merit from its response to environment is the central question of a breeding programme.
In ASReml
asreml(yield ~ env, random = ~ gen + diag(env):gen)
In flexyBayes
The same, with backend = “brms”: the structured genotype-by-environment terms are a brms capability.
What the posterior adds
Heritability, a ratio of variance components, is computed on the draws rather than through the delta method.
What it costs
The factor-analytic model, the workhorse of large METs, is refused by both engines. Section 5 says what that means in practice.

1. The MET question

agridat::yan.winterwheat is 18 winter wheat genotypes across 9 Ontario environments, one yield per combination.

library(flexyBayes)
yw <- agridat::yan.winterwheat
table(nlevels(yw$gen), nlevels(yw$env))
#>     
#>      9
#>   18 1

Three models answer three different questions, and they nest.

Main effect only. random = ~ gen says varieties differ but rank the same everywhere. One variance component.

Plus interaction. random = ~ gen + gen:env says varieties also respond differently to environment, and measures that with a second component. The ratio of the two is the question a breeder asks: how much of the varietal signal survives across sites.

Heterogeneous by environment. random = ~ diag(env):gen says the genotype spread itself differs between environments – a high-yielding site may separate varieties more than a stressed one.

2. Main effect plus interaction 

fit <- flexybayes(yield ~ env, random = ~ gen + gen:env, data = yw,
                  backend = "brms", chains = 2L, n_samples = 1500L,
                  warmup = 750L, seed = 1L, verbose = FALSE,
                  mcmc_verbose = FALSE)
#> Warning: There were 163 divergent transitions after warmup. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#divergent-transitions-after-warmup

tidy(fit, effects = "random")
#>         term  estimate  std.error   conf.low conf.high
#> 1     sd_gen 0.4039935 0.09089507 0.26661810 0.6089082
#> 2 sd_gen:env 0.2559709 0.12131913 0.01657049 0.4170231
#> 3      sigma 0.2426789 0.11766439 0.06811196 0.4099759

sd_gen is the spread of general merit, sd_gen:env the spread of environment-specific deviation. When the second is comparable to the first, selecting on an overall mean discards real information.

Heritability on an entry-mean basis follows from the components:

vc <- tidy(fit, effects = "random")
g  <- function(nm) vc$estimate[vc$term == nm]
n_env <- nlevels(yw$env)
g("sd_gen")^2 /
  (g("sd_gen")^2 + g("sd_gen:env")^2 / n_env + g("sigma")^2 / n_env)
#> [1] 0.9219147

Under REML this ratio needs the delta method for an interval. Under a posterior the same computation done draw by draw gives one directly.

3. Heterogeneous genotype variance

diag(env):gen gives each environment its own genotype variance and no correlation between them.

fit_d <- flexybayes(yield ~ env, random = ~ diag(env):gen, data = yw,
                    backend = "brms", chains = 2L, n_samples = 1500L,
                    warmup = 750L, seed = 1L, verbose = FALSE,
                    mcmc_verbose = FALSE)
#> Warning: There were 1 divergent transitions after warmup. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#divergent-transitions-after-warmup
#> to find out why this is a problem and how to eliminate them.
#> Warning: There were 2 chains where the estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information was low. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bfmi-low
#> Warning: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
#> Warning: Bulk Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior means and medians may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bulk-ess
#> Warning: Tail Effective Samples Size (ESS) is too low, indicating posterior variances and tail quantiles may be unreliable.
#> Running the chains for more iterations may help. See
#> https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#tail-ess
#> Warning: There were 1 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing
#> adapt_delta above 0.8 may help. See
#> http://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#divergent-transitions-after-warmup
#> Warning: flexyBayes: the sampler may not have converged -- min effective sample
#> size 85. Treat the posterior with caution: increase `warmup` / `n_samples`,
#> raise `control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)` where the run reported divergent
#> transitions, simplify the model, or supply a more informative prior. Inspect
#> the full diagnostics with summary(). Silence this warning via
#> options(flexyBayes.silence_convergence_warning = TRUE).
head(tidy(fit_d, effects = "random"), 5)
#>              term  estimate std.error   conf.low conf.high
#> 1 sd_gen__envBH93 0.5342711 0.1621136 0.23094362 0.8780886
#> 2 sd_gen__envEA93 0.3054336 0.1544874 0.01734686 0.6259545
#> 3 sd_gen__envHW93 0.4195316 0.1657817 0.08295558 0.7453970
#> 4 sd_gen__envID93 0.2524538 0.1477405 0.01362567 0.5497107
#> 5 sd_gen__envKE93 0.6555202 0.1714498 0.36326968 1.0337423

One standard deviation per environment. Environments with a larger value discriminate between varieties more strongly.

us(env):gen goes further and estimates the correlations between environments as well, which is what tells you whether two sites are effectively repeats of each other. It costs a parameter for every pair.

4. Known relationship matrices

Genomic selection replaces “genotypes are independent draws” with “genotypes are related, and the relationship matrix says how”. vm(gen, K) supplies that matrix; ped(animal, A) is the same term spelled for a pedigree.

set.seed(4)
n_g  <- 40
M    <- matrix(rbinom(n_g * 200, 2, 0.3), nrow = n_g)
Ks   <- scale(M)
K    <- tcrossprod(Ks) / ncol(Ks)
diag(K) <- diag(K) + 1e-6
dimnames(K) <- list(paste0("g", 1:n_g), paste0("g", 1:n_g))

dg <- data.frame(gen = factor(rep(paste0("g", 1:n_g), each = 3),
                              levels = paste0("g", 1:n_g)),
                 env = factor(rep(1:3, times = n_g)))
u  <- as.numeric(crossprod(chol(K), rnorm(n_g)))
dg$yield <- 5 + u[as.integer(dg$gen)] + rnorm(nrow(dg), 0, 0.4)

# INLA is given the precision, its documented carrier for this term
Q <- solve(K)
fit_g <- flexybayes(yield ~ env,
                    random = ~ vm(gen, cov = fb_cov(Q, type = "precision")),
                    data = dg, known_matrices = list(Q = Q),
                    backend = "inla", verbose = FALSE)
tidy(fit_g, effects = "random")
#>        term  estimate  std.error  conf.low conf.high
#> 1     sigma 0.4234619 0.03438988 0.3610958 0.4958863
#> 2 sd_gen_id 0.9634456 0.12168364 0.7507251 1.2273814

The two engines take the relationship in different forms, and naming the wrong one refuses rather than converting silently. INLA works from the precision – the inverse of the relationship matrix – because its latent field is parameterised that way and a sparse precision is what makes the fit affordable. brms takes the covariance directly:

flexybayes(yield ~ env, random = ~ vm(gen, K), data = dg,
           known_matrices = list(K = K), backend = "brms")

fb_cov() names the carrier: covariance, precision, chol, blocks or low_rank. backend = "auto" picks an engine that accepts the carrier you supplied.

The random effect is now correlated across genotypes according to K, so a genotype with no phenotype of its own still receives a prediction through its relatives. That is genomic prediction.

5. What is refused, and what to do instead

Model class Spelling INLA brms
Factor-analytic genotype-by-environment covariance ~ fa(env, k):gen refuses refuses
Heterogeneous variances with one shared correlation ~ corh(f):g refuses refuses
Multi-trait covariance ~ us(trait):vm(gen) refuses refuses
Unstructured genotype-by-environment covariance ~ us(f):g refuses fits
Known-covariance genomic / pedigree random effect ~ vm(g, K), ~ ped(a, A) fits fits

The factor-analytic model is the significant gap. fa(env, k):gen approximates the environment covariance by a rank-k loading matrix plus a diagonal, and it is the standard tool for a MET with many sites, because us() becomes unaffordable. Neither engine emits it.

Where a MET is small enough, us(env):gen gives the full covariance and diag(env):gen the heterogeneous-variance approximation. Where it is not, ASReml remains the tool for the factor-analytic fit, and a flexyBayes fit of a reduced model can be compared against it.

6. Pitfalls

The relationship matrix must match the factor levels. Row and column order of K has to correspond to levels(gen). A mismatch is a silent reordering of the genotypes.

Positive definiteness. A genomic relationship matrix built from markers is often singular. Adding a small ridge to the diagonal, as above, is the usual remedy and the validator will refuse without it.

Interaction terms are brms-only. gen:env refuses on INLA, which collapses the finest stratum. auto routes it.

Heritability needs its basis stated. Entry-mean and plot basis differ by the divisors in the denominator. Report which one.
